20.0.0.en: As a result of the quarrel between the men of Judah and Israel (ch. 19), a wicked man of the tribe of Benjamin took advantage of the situation by declaring separation from David's kingdom, and incited the tribes not to follow David but to return to their homes.

20.0.1.en: The discussion began as a show of zeal for enthroning David but ended in separation between the tribes. This teaches us not to enter into a discussion that is pointless and may even lead to the opposite of what is hoped from it. The Apostle Paul said: "But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes" (2 Tim 2:23). So do not argue with an angry person, but absorb his anger with your love and patience, and you will draw him and spare yourself many problems.

20.1.0.en: Sheba's call found attentive ears among all the tribes, for as soon as he called them they answered his call and left their allegiance to the king, following this wicked man, declaring thereby their revolt against David's rule, and none remained loyal to him except the tribe of Judah, which accompanied him until his entry into Jerusalem. Thus we see the quick fickleness of the mind of the crowds.

20.1.1.en: God allowed this as discipline for David, who had wavered in his relationship with God when he sinned in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.

20.2.0.en: The king reached his house in Jerusalem, and shut up his ten concubines whom he had left to keep his palace, and with whom Absalom had lain (ch. 16:22); he did not live with them, because it was not fitting, and he treated them with honor, and they lived out their lives in chastity.

20.3.s.en: (2) David commissions Amasa and Abishai to deal with Sheba

20.3.0.en: David had appointed Amasa commander of his army after removing Joab, because he was troubled by his actions, and he charged him to assemble an army from the tribe of Judah within three days and then return to him in Jerusalem.

20.4.0.en: Amasa obeyed, but it seems that matters did not go as expected, for the three days passed without his returning at the time David had set for him.

20.5.0.en: David saw, with his leader's shrewdness, that it was not wise to wait any longer for Amasa's return, for his delay gave the enemy, Sheba son of Bichri, room to arrange his ranks and occupy fortified places so that it would be hard to seize him, so he charged Abishai to take the king's special guard and go to pursue Sheba, for David expected that Sheba's rebellion would be more dangerous than Absalom's rebellion.

20.6.0.en: Abishai carried out the king's command and took the soldiers, heroes of wars, who had been under Joab's leadership, among them David's special guard and the battalions of infantry, and they went out of Jerusalem to go after Sheba and fight him.

20.6.1.en: It is not wise to be lazy and slow in facing the enemy, Satan; rather, sin must be cut off quickly, lest it grow within a person and become hard to resist. So drive out the thought from its beginning and do not be lax about evil talk, so that you do not fall into wicked deeds.

20.7.0.en: Gibeon: a city north of Jerusalem about 8 km away from it.

20.7.1.en: On their march they came to a famous rock in Gibeon, and there they met Amasa returning with the soldiers he had gathered and heading for Jerusalem to meet the king. Joab accompanied his brother Abishai, and he was wearing his war clothes, and over his garment a girdle with a sword fastened to it, and Joab had deliberately made the fastening loose so that it would fall, and Joab would take hold of it with his left hand as though he did not want the sword to fall to the ground, but in truth he was preparing to deal treacherously with Amasa, as will appear.

20.8.0.en: Joab received Amasa with feigned affection, asking after his welfare, and took hold of his beard with his right hand to kiss him, as was the custom of close friends at that time.

20.9.0.en: Joab was holding Amasa's beard with his right hand to kiss him, and in his left hand the sword that had slipped from its fastening to the girdle, and Amasa did not expect treachery from Joab, so Joab struck him with the sword in the belly with a single blow that killed him at once, and then Joab and Abishai went after Sheba to put an end to his rebellion. Here appear Joab's jealousy and his grudge against Amasa, because David had set him up as commander of the army in his place, and this was because of Joab's harshness in his words to David, in addition to his treachery in killing Abner before, and also the killing of Absalom, and now he adds another crime to his crimes by killing an innocent man, Amasa, so he deserved punishment at the hand of Solomon the son of David.

20.9.1.en: Do not run after positions and honor, lest you clash with others and hold a grudge against them and live in gloom and misery; rather seek the Kingdom of God and trust that He will give you peace and honor, so that you live happier than all those around you.

20.10.s.en: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

20.10.0.en: The soldiers were lingering in their march at the body of Amasa, so one of Joab's followers stood beside the body, and his task was to urge the soldiers not to linger but to keep marching behind Joab, and in partiality to Joab he coupled Joab's name with David's name, proclaiming that he was still the commander of the armies and not Amasa, though this was not true, but this plan succeeded and the soldiers followed Joab.

20.11.0.en: Amasa lay on the roadside, wallowing in his blood, and everyone who passed him was affected by the horror of the sight and hesitated to continue marching, so when the man, Joab's follower, saw that the presence of Amasa's body was delaying the soldiers from following Joab, he moved the body into a field away from the road and covered it with a garment, and the soldiers' march became orderly, without stopping, behind Joab to go after Sheba son of Bichri.

20.12.0.en: Abel of Beth-maachah: a fortified city in the land of the tribe of Naphtali. It is now a small village lying northwest of Lake Huleh.

20.12.1.en: During the army's march behind Joab, many were joining it from the tribes until it reached a city called "Abel of Beth-maachah," in which Sheba son of Bichri had fortified himself, and there joined him members of a large family famous in that region, the "Berites."

20.13.0.en: Mound: a barrier or wall of stones and earth.

20.13.1.en: The commanders of David's army learned from their own reconnaissance sources that Sheba son of Bichri and his men were in the city of "Ayil Beth-maachah," so they besieged it to seize him and set up mounds around it, and prevented people from entering and leaving the city. After a period of siege, David's men began to open breaches in the wall to be able to enter the city.

20.14.0.en: At this time, when it seemed that the city was exposed to invasion and destruction, a wise woman appeared who was the cause of her city being spared the destruction that threatened it. That woman called to Joab's soldiers to ask him to come near the wall so that she could speak with him.

20.15.0.en: Joab responded to her request, and she asked him whether he was Joab and whether he was ready to hear what she would say, and he answered yes, and she spoke to him with respect and humility, saying "thine handmaid," that is, your servant.

20.16.0.en: The woman began her speech by mentioning what the wise men of her city "Abel" were famous for, how everyone who sought counsel resorted to them and they solved their problems and judged the cases brought before them. Their opinion was always sound and ended the problem in the best way, so she invited Joab to reach an understanding as the Law commands (Deut 20:10) and not to rush into destroying the city so as not to do evil.

20.17.0.en: The woman speaks on behalf of her city, saying that it is a city that loves peace and is faithful to the people of Israel, and you, Joab, have come with your armies to destroy and wipe out a city that is a mother in Israel (so called because of the wisdom of its people). Then the woman went on to say, why do you seek to destroy one of the cities of the Lord, which He gave as an inheritance to His people?!

20.18.0.en: Joab answered that he did not allow himself to destroy and ruin, and that the matter was not as she had presented it, for all there was, was that a man named Sheba son of Bichri from the region of the hill country of Ephraim had declared his rebellion against the king and revolted against him, and if the people of her city delivered him to him, he would depart at once and lift the siege from it. The woman answered him that if that was so, the people of her city would seize Sheba and kill him and throw his head over the wall.

20.19.0.en: The woman went to the people of the city and persuaded them by her wisdom that they should spare their city destruction and ruin rather than shelter one rebellious and disobedient person, and being sensible, they seized Sheba and killed him and threw his head to Joab from over the wall. Then Joab blew the trumpet, giving his soldiers the signal to end the war, and they departed to their country, and Joab returned to King David in Jerusalem. Thus God allowed this rebellion as discipline for David for his old sin, but He ended the trouble quickly by the killing of Sheba, for God wants us to understand His discipline and repent, and it is not His pleasure that we fall into hard sufferings.

20.19.1.en: The intervention of the wise by their wisdom spares many difficult situations. So let us be positive in confronting events and act with the wisdom with which God favors us in dealing with matters, so that we may be messengers of peace in the environment in which we live; for wisdom, as the Book of Proverbs describes it, "is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and happy is every one that retaineth her" (Prov 3:18).

20.20.s.en: (5) David's appointment of religious, military and administrative heads

20.20.0.en: The Cherethites and the Pelethites: the Cherethites are the police and the royal guard, and the Pelethites are the infantry of the army.

20.20.1.en: As a reward for his victory in the matter of Sheba son of Bichri, David pardoned Joab and restored him to the command of the army and confirmed him in his position, and David also set Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the royal guard and the infantry of the army.

20.21.0.en: Adoram: a man whom David set to oversee the collection of tribute, and he remained in this office throughout the reign of Solomon and until the time of Rehoboam.

20.21.1.en: Tribute: the tax imposed on the other peoples, not the people of the Lord, who were subject to David's authority.

20.21.2.en: Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud: he held the office of recorder in the reign of David and Solomon.

20.21.3.en: David appointed Adoram to oversee the collection of tribute from the foreign peoples subject to him, and he appointed Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud to record the laws, regulations, administrative decisions and judicial rulings.

20.22.0.en: Sheva: a scribe in the reign of King David.

20.22.1.en: David appointed Sheva secretary of the kingdom and the one responsible for overseeing the accounts of the state.

20.22.2.en: Zadok and Abiathar were great priests, and Zadok was of the descendants of Eleazar son of Aaron and Abiathar of the descendants of Ithamar son of Aaron, and he was the son of Ahimelech whom Saul killed in the massacre of the priests (1 Sam 22:20).

20.23.0.en: A priest to David: that is, a special counselor, and not a priest performing the works of the priesthood in the house of the Lord.

20.23.1.en: David appointed Ira the Jairite as a special counselor to him, who would present to him the wishes of his people, and through whom the king would convey his directions to the officials in his government.

20.23.2.en: It is good that our life be organized and that there be someone in charge of each responsibility, subject to him, so that matters may proceed in peace. May you, if you are in charge, distribute the responsibilities to others and show compassion to them, and on the other hand submit to everyone in charge, so that your life may proceed in stability.

20.23.3.en: The right of the Gibeonites and the wars with the Philistines

21.0.s.en: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

21.0.0.en: Enquired of the LORD: God's help and guidance.

21.0.1.en: The Gibeonites: the inhabitants of the city of Gibeon, which is 8 km north of Jerusalem, and they belong to the Amorites, and made a covenant with Joshua (Josh 9). A famine occurred in the land of Israel that lasted three years, so David prayed to the Lord, and He informed him that the famine was a divine punishment because of the treachery of Saul and the people toward the Gibeonites and his killing of some of them despite the covenant between them and Joshua. Although Joshua had erred in making the covenant with them, the covenant made in the name of the Lord must be respected or He will be angry, and perhaps the people rejoiced at taking over the land of the Gibeonites, as being part of the lands inhabited by pagans that ought to be taken by the people of God, forgetting God's covenant that Joshua made with them.

21.1.0.en: David set about appeasing the Gibeonites, so he called their leaders and asked them what he should do for them.

21.2.0.en: The Gibeonites were a peaceful people, so they answered David that Saul had not taken from them money, gold or silver for which they should demand restitution from his heirs, and that they had no authority over the children of Israel that they might take vengeance on them by killing one or some of them; moreover the children of Israel at the present time had not wronged them. David told them to ask what they wished and he would carry out their request, in order to appease God, as we mentioned. This shows that the Gibeonites were influenced by their association with the children of Israel, so they became peaceful and not attached to money or exploitative of others.

21.3.0.en: Gibeah of Saul: it is the same as Gibeah of Benjamin and was the capital of the kingdom in the days of Saul, and it is present-day Tell el-Ful, 6 km north of Jerusalem.

21.3.1.en: The Gibeonites said that what would satisfy them was the killing of seven of the descendants of Saul, who had killed many of them and tried to exterminate them, and then hanging the bodies of the seven in the capital of Saul's kingdom, which was Gibeah of Benjamin, and David agreed. Here the Gibeonites did not ask for silver or gold, because the principle known from ancient times is that blood is redeemed by blood and not by money (Gen 9:6, Num 35:31). They did not name particular persons from Saul's descendants because they knew David's covenant with Jonathan not to destroy his offspring, so they left him to choose any seven. David erred in not asking God whether He agreed to the killing and hanging of the seven or not.

21.4.0.en: Mephibosheth, who was handed over to the Gibeonites with the other six, was a direct son of Saul, and is different from Mephibosheth son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, whom David did not wish to hand over, in order to keep the old promise he had made to Jonathan his father not to kill any of his children.

21.5.0.en: Rizpah the daughter of Aiah: Saul's concubine, on account of whom a quarrel arose between Ish-bosheth and Abner that led to Abner's joining David.

21.5.1.en: Armoni and Mephibosheth: two sons of Saul by his concubine Rizpah, whom the Gibeonites killed with five others of Saul's family.

21.5.2.en: Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite: Saul gave him in marriage his eldest daughter Merab, whom he had promised to David.

21.5.3.en: The sons of Saul whom King David handed over to the Gibeonites were:

21.5.4.en: Two sons of Saul by his concubine Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, namely Armoni and Mephibosheth, and five who were the sons of Michal, whom her sister Merab bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai (1 Sam 18:19), and she adopted them after her sister's death.

21.6.0.en: The Gibeonites killed the seven sons of Saul and hanged them on one of the mountains, and that was at the beginning of the barley harvest season, that is, in the month of May. This shows God's justice on account of Saul's many evils against God, David and the Gibeonites, and because he did not give Merab his daughter to David as he had promised him but gave her to Adriel. And if some of these sons were pious, torment will not touch them in eternity.

21.7.0.en: Rizpah the daughter of Aiah grieved over the hanging of her two sons, so she set about honoring their bodies by spreading for herself coarse cloth to sit on upon the same rock on which they were hanged, and to guard the bodies so that birds of prey would not devour them, and she continued her guard until the Lord pardoned the people and had mercy on them and the rain fell, and she took the bodies down. Rizpah remained grieving in austerity, sitting on sackcloth, probably for many days until the rain fell as a declaration that God had lifted His anger and the famine was over, although the Jewish Law provides for taking down hanged bodies before evening (Deut 21:22); but this was a special case, for those who hanged these were the Gibeonites, who were not Jews and therefore not bound by the Law.

21.7.1.en: The falling of rain in the days of harvest, that is, in the months of April and May, is unusual, but God allowed it as a declaration of the ending of the famine and His pleasure with His repentant people, and He did not wait until October or November, in which the rains fall, for it would be hard for the bodies to remain hanging throughout those months.

21.8.0.en: Jabesh-gilead: a city on Mount Gilead east of the Jordan, 16 km southeast of Beth-shan, now Tell Abu Kharaz north of Wadi Yabis.

21.8.1.en: Beth-shan: a city 8 km west of the Jordan River, whose site is now Tell el-Husn.

21.8.2.en: Gilboa: the northeastern part of Mount Ephraim.

21.8.3.en: David learned what Rizpah had endured of toil for the sake of honoring the bodies and preserving them, so he also shared in this honoring by taking the bodies of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead to bury them, for the men of Jabesh-gilead had crossed the Jordan and stolen their bodies after they were killed in the war with the Philistines (1 Sam 31:11, 12).

21.9.0.en: The bones of those hanged: what is meant is their bodies, for it is not possible for all bodies to decay so quickly.

21.9.1.en: Zelah: a city in the land of the tribe of Benjamin (now Khirbet Salah northwest of Jerusalem). David also took the bodies of the seven who had been hanged and buried them all with honor in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father, in the city of "Zelah" neighboring "Gibeah," and by this David proved that the killing of the seven sons of Saul was not out of grudge on his part against them, but he had been compelled to do this act of atonement so that the Lord might be pleased with His people. The Lord had declared the end of His anger by the falling of rain to water the land, and so the famine ended.

21.10.0.en: A new war arose between Israel and the Philistines, and David went down to the battle to share the fighting with his soldiers, as kings used to do in ancient times, but he felt great exhaustion, for he was over sixty years of age and had endured many troubles in his life.

21.11.0.en: Ishbi-benob: one of the sons of Rapha, a Philistine giant who was about to kill David, but Abishai hastened and killed him before he came near David.

21.11.1.en: Three hundred shekels of brass: that is, about 5 kg.

21.11.2.en: Being girded with a new one: that is, girded with a new sword.

21.11.3.en: "Ishbi-benob," a son of Goliath the giant whom David killed in his youth, was among the Philistine warriors, and the weight of his spear was about 5 kg and his weapon was new. This soldier recognized David's person in the field and noticed that he was tired, so he thought it would be easy to attack him and kill him. But Abishai the brother of Joab noticed what was going on around the king and hastened to his aid and was able to kill that soldier. After this event David's men who were loyal to him swore that they would not let him go out to the wars with them any more, because he was considered an important symbol for his people and his life was a precious treasure for his men, and his being killed in any battle would mean the defeat of the whole people.

21.12.0.en: Gob: it is the same as Gezer, a city near Lachish bordering the land of Ephraim, and now called Tell el-Jazar, 30 km northwest of Jerusalem.

21.12.1.en: Sibbechai the Hushathite: one of the heroes of King David, and he is the one who killed "Saph," one of the sons of Rapha. Saph: one of the sons of Rapha, one of the Philistine giants, and he is also called "Sippai" (1 Chr 20:4). The war with the Philistines was a series of successive battles, no sooner had one ended than another began. The next battlefield was "Gob," and in this battle Sibbechai, one of David's heroes, killed "Saph," one of the Philistine giants and a son of "Rapha," one of the Philistine commanders.

21.13.0.en: Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite: he is the one who slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite.

21.13.1.en: The previous battle at "Gob" had hardly ended when another battle broke out in the same place, in which the name of another of David's heroes shone, "Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim," for he killed a giant from the city of Gath named Goliath, the staff of whose spear was as long as the beam used in weaving. This Goliath is another person than the one David killed in his youth; perhaps he was his brother and was named after him in memory of him, and his real name is Lahmi, as mentioned in (1 Chr 20:5).

21.14.0.en: Another battle took place at Gath, one of the five great Philistine cities, in which appeared a Philistine of strange stature, the fingers and toes of whose hands and feet were twenty-four in number and not twenty as with any ordinary person, and he also was a son of "Rapha," and he appeared defying the Jews as the old Goliath had done, taunting the children of Israel, which kindled the zeal of Jonathan the son of Shimeah, David's brother, who is "Shammah" as mentioned in (1 Sam 16:9), and he killed him.

21.15.0.en: In the battles mentioned, four of the strongest Philistine soldiers were killed by the hand of David's heroes, and these four are:

21.15.4.en: 4- The man with twenty-four fingers and toes, whom Jonathan killed; and these four are the sons of "Rapha" who was of "Gath."

21.15.5.en: And when it says "fell by the hand of David," it means by this his men, for David is the commander of the armies and his men are the ones who killed the heroes of the Philistines.

21.15.6.en: The Lord always stands by His children as long as they hold fast to Him, and guards them and gives them victory in wars, whether they are wars between men or spiritual wars stirred up against them by the enemy of good. Let us know that victory in all circumstances is from the Lord, so let us trust in Him and not be troubled because of the threats around us, and lift our hearts in prayer, confident of His protection of us.
